Florida Arbovirus Surveillance 
Week 40: October 4-10, 2026 
 
Arbovirus surveillance in Florida includes endemic mosquito-borne viruses such as West Nile virus (WNV), 
Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), and St. Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV), as well as exotic viruses 
such as dengue virus (DENV), chikungunya virus (CHIKV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and California encephalitis group 
viruses (CEV). Malaria, a parasitic mosquito-borne disease, is also included. During the period of October 4-
10, 2026, the following arboviral activity was recorded in Florida. 
 
WNV activity: No human cases of WNV infection were reported this week. No horses with WNV infection were 
reported this week. Thirty-nine sentinel chickens tested positive for antibodies to WNV in Alachua, Bay, Duval, 
Hernando, Indian River, Leon, Manatee, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas, Polk, St. Lucie, Sumter, and 
Walton counties. In 2026, positive samples from five symptomatic humans, two asymptomatic blood donors, 
316 sentinel chickens, two horses, and eight mosquito pools have been reported from 27 counties. 
 
SLEV activity: No human cases of SLEV infection were reported this week. One sentinel chicken tested 
positive for antibodies to SLEV in Martin County. In 2026, two sentinel chickens have been reported from two 
counties. 
 
EEEV activity: One human case of EEEV infection was reported this week. No horses with EEEV infection 
were reported this week. One sentinel chicken tested positive for antibodies to EEEV in Leon County. In 2026, 
positive samples from one human, 45 sentinel chickens, and seven horses have been reported from 17 
counties. 
 
International Travel-Associated Dengue: Twenty-six cases of dengue were reported this week. In 2026, 288 
travel-associated dengue cases have been reported. 
 
Dengue Cases Acquired in Florida: Seventy-two cases of locally acquired dengue were reported this week. 
In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties. 
 
International Travel-Associated Chikungunya Fever Cases: Six cases of chikungunya fever were reported 
this week. In 2026, 84 cases of travel-associated chikungunya fever have been reported. 
 
Chikungunya Fever Cases Acquired in Florida: No cases of locally acquired chikungunya fever were 
reported this week. In 2026, one case of locally acquired chikungunya fever has been reported from one 
county. 
 
International Travel-Associated Oropouche Fever cases: No cases of Oropouche fever were reported this 
week. In 2026, no cases of travel-associated Oropouche fever have been reported. 
 
International Travel-Associated Zika Fever Cases: No cases of Zika fever were reported this week. In 2026, 
no travel-associated Zika fever cases have been reported. 
 
Zika Fever Cases Acquired in Florida: No cases of locally acquired Zika fever were reported this week. In 
2026, no cases of locally acquired Zika fever have been reported.  
 
Advisories/Alerts as of October 10, 2026: Bay, Brevard, Broward, Holmes, Leon, Manatee, Martin, Palm 
Beach, Polk, and Walton counties are currently under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. Alachua, Duval, 
Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Pasco, and Pinellas counties are currently under a mosquito-borne illness 
alert.

2026 Human Case Summary 
 
2026 West Nile Virus Illness Acquired in Florida: In 2026, five human cases of WNV illness acquired in 
Florida have been reported in Alachua (May, August), Duval (August), Holmes (August), and Walton (July) 
counties. Two asymptomatic blood donors have been reported in Duval (August) and Leon (July) counties. 
 
2026 Eastern Equine Encephalitis Acquired in Florida: In 2026, one human case of EEEV illness acquired 
in Florida has been reported in Leon County (September). 
 
2026 International Travel-Associated Chikungunya Cases: Eighty-four cases with onset in 2026 have been 
reported in individuals with travel history to a chikungunya-endemic area in the two weeks prior to onset. 
Counties reporting cases were: Alachua, Broward (4), Collier (2), Hernando, Hillsborough (8), Lee, Miami-Dade 
(52), Monroe (2), Okaloosa, Orange (3), Osceola, Palm Beach (4), Pinellas, Seminole, St. Lucie, and St. 
Johns. Countries of origin were Bolivia (2), Brazil (2), Cameroon, Cuba (53), Guyana, Nicaragua (23), Sri 
Lanka, and Surinam. One case was reported in a non-Florida resident. 
 
2026 Chikungunya Cases Acquired in Florida: One case of locally acquired chikungunya fever has been 
reported in Miami-Dade County with onset in August. 
 
2026 International Travel-Associated Dengue Cases: Two hundred eighty-eight cases with onset in 2026 
have been reported in individuals with travel to a dengue-endemic area in the two weeks prior to onset. 
Counties reporting cases were: Alachua, Bay, Brevard (2), Broward (20), Collier (4), Duval (2), Hendry, 
Hillsborough (15), Lake, Lee (13), Manatee (2), Marion, Miami-Dade (182), Monroe, Orange (7), Osceola (3), 
Palm Beach (13), Pasco, Pinellas (2), Polk (4), Sarasota, Seminole (3), St. Johns, St. Lucie (6), and Walton. 
Six cases were reported in non-Florida residents. In 2026, 254 cases of dengue reported in Florida have been 
serotyped by PCR. Please see the table below for a breakdown of cases by country of origin and serotype.

Mosquito Pools

Dead Birds 
 
The Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) collects reports of dead birds, which can be an 
indication of arbovirus circulation in an area. This week, 27 reports representing a total of 59 dead birds, 
including one crow, two raptors, and four doves, were received from 16 counties. 
 
In 2026, 1487 reports representing a total of 3427 dead birds (78 crows, 29 jays, 412 raptors, 173 doves) were 
received from 54 of Florida’s 67 counties.

Case tallies included in the weekly Florida arbovirus surveillance report include confirmed and probable cases for EEE, 
WNV infection, SLE, dengue, chikungunya, and malaria by date of onset.  Suspect cases are not included. Activity is 
mapped by county of exposure rather than county of residence. Case definitions being used in Florida are consistent with 
national criteria provided by the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) and may be viewed at: 
www.floridahealth.gov/diseases-and-conditions/disease-reporting-and-management/disease-reporting-and-
surveillance/index.html. Case tallies reported by CDC do not include suspect cases and cases are reported by patient state 
of residence rather than where the exposure occurred. Data is provided by county health departments, Department of 
Health Bureau of Public Health Laboratories, Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, mosquito control 
agencies, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, medical providers and veterinarians. Equine cases are 
provided by the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.
